Categorising invoices into the correct General Ledger (GL) code is fundamental for accurate financial reporting and tax compliance. GL codes are accounting categories used to track different types of expenses and revenues. Miscategorisation can lead to financial misstatements, compliance issues, and increased audit risk, making accurate classification essential for businesses. Although artificial intelligence is increasingly used to automate such tasks, most prior work has focused on large language models (LLMs) or rule-based systems, which can be costly, less interpretable, or raise data privacy concerns. In contrast, small language models (SLMs) have received less attention for financial document classification, despite their potential for in-house deployment, cost efficiency, and enhanced data security. The research gap addressed in this work is the lack of systematic study on whether in-house SLMs can match or exceed LLM performance for invoice GL code classification, and how the geometric properties of their embeddings contribute to this performance. To our knowledge, this is the first large-scale analysis of SLM embedding geometry and its impact on real-world invoice GL code classification.

We focus on SLMs—specifically, the Sentence-BERT (SBERT) model and DeBERTa (Decoding-enhanced BERT with Disentangled Attention)—which are more manageable for in-house deployment compared to LLMs. SBERT is a sentence transformer designed to generate semantically meaningful sentence embeddings, while DeBERTa is a transformer-based model known for its strong performance on language understanding tasks. We selected these models due to their balance of interpretability, resource efficiency, and strong performance in prior text classification benchmarks. While both models were evaluated, we report detailed results for SBERT, which consistently outperformed DeBERTa in our experiments. For completeness, DeBERTa achieved 0.92 accuracy and 0.85 F1 score on the test set, with a macro-averaged F1 of 0.83 (see Supplementary Table S1).

We begin by analysing the pre-trained embedding geometry of these models on a financial invoice corpus. Here, "embedding geometry" refers to how sentence representations are arranged in the model’s high-dimensional vector space. "Anisotropy" means that most embeddings are crowded along certain directions, while "isotropy" means they are more evenly spread out. Global anisotropy can hinder the model’s ability to distinguish between classes, whereas local isotropy—especially within clusters associated with vendors—enables better separation and classification of invoices. We observe that the embedding space is globally anisotropic but contains locally isotropic clusters, which are strongly correlated with vendor identity. This suggests that vendor information is a key driver of semantic similarity in invoice texts, extending prior findings at the token level to sentence embeddings in a financial context.

Our dataset comprises approximately 8,000 invoices from over 100 clients and 200 vendors, covering 25 distinct GL codes. These 25 codes were selected as the most frequently used by our client base and represent a substantial subset of all possible codes, capturing the majority of real-world invoice categorisation scenarios encountered in practice. To ensure diversity and quality, we included invoices from a wide range of industries and performed manual checks to verify label accuracy. The manual verification involved two annotators with accounting backgrounds independently reviewing a random 10% sample of the dataset; disagreements were resolved through discussion, resulting in an inter-annotator agreement of 0.93 (Cohen’s kappa). Preprocessing steps included lowercasing all text, removing extraneous whitespace, standardising date and currency formats, and replacing missing or incomplete fields with a placeholder token. Invoices with missing critical fields (e.g., vendor or amount) were excluded from the dataset. The data was randomly split into training (70%, 5,600 invoices), validation (15%, 1,200 invoices), and test (15%, 1,200 invoices) sets to evaluate model performance and generalisation; no cross-validation was performed due to computational constraints and the need to maintain a fixed test set for fair comparison with baselines. While we aimed for broad industry representation, some sectors (e.g., technology, retail) are more heavily represented, and certain vendors appear more frequently, which may introduce bias and affect generalisability to underrepresented industries or rare vendors. The moderate class imbalance (largest class 14%, smallest 2%) and overrepresentation of certain industries/vendors could lead to reduced performance on minority classes or less common sectors, and this is reflected in the per-class F1 scores. Table 2 shows the distribution of GL codes in the dataset.

Table 2: Distribution of GL Codes in the Dataset (Top 5 Shown)

| GL Code | Count | Percentage |
|---------|-------|------------|
| Office Supplies | 1,120 | 14% |
| IT Services     | 1,040 | 13% |
| Travel          | 960  | 12% |
| Marketing       | 800  | 10% |
| Consulting      | 720  | 9%  |
| ...             | ...  | ... |
| Smallest class  | 160  | 2%  |

SBERT was fine-tuned using a cross-entropy loss for multi-class classification, with a learning rate of 2e-5, batch size of 32, and early stopping based on validation loss. Training was conducted for up to 10 epochs, with the best model selected via validation F1 score. Hyperparameters were tuned using grid search on the validation set. SBERT, fine-tuned on a single GPU, achieves 0.96 accuracy (±0.01) and 0.90 F1 score (±0.02) on the test set for invoice classification across the 25 GL code classes. The F1 score was calculated as the harmonic mean of precision and recall on the test split, providing a balanced measure of classification performance. The dataset exhibits moderate class imbalance, with some GL codes representing as little as 2% of the data. To further support claims of generalisability, we also report a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.88, indicating strong performance across all classes, including minority ones. Per-class F1 scores ranged from 0.81 to 0.94, with lower scores generally corresponding to the smallest classes. For comparison, a zero-shot LLM baseline—using a commercial API (OpenAI GPT-3.5) prompted with: "Given the following invoice text, assign the most appropriate GL code from the following list: [list of GL codes]. Invoice: [invoice text]"—achieved 0.82 accuracy (±0.02) and 0.75 F1 (±0.03), with a macro-averaged F1 of 0.72. A vendor identity-only baseline (assigning the most frequent GL code for each vendor) achieved 0.78 accuracy (±0.02) and 0.68 F1 (±0.03), with a macro-averaged F1 of 0.65. All baselines used the same data splits and preprocessing as SBERT to ensure fair comparison. Notably, SBERT shows improved performance on smaller, more challenging categories and for new clients, demonstrating promising generalisation. Statistical significance testing was performed using paired bootstrap resampling with 10,000 resamples to estimate 95% confidence intervals for accuracy and F1; SBERT’s improvements over both baselines were significant (p < 0.01).

The connection between embedding geometry and classification outcomes is evident: the presence of locally isotropic clusters associated with vendors aligns with higher classification accuracy, indicating that the model leverages these geometric structures for decision-making. To further probe model behaviour, we experimented with "structured input"—explicitly formatted invoice information designed to aid human readers, such as tabular layouts or labeled fields (e.g., "Vendor:", "Amount:", "Description:"). The rationale was that structured formats might help the model focus on key fields and reduce ambiguity, potentially improving performance, especially for invoices with less regular text. We tested both fully tabular formats and semi-structured labeled fields. Quantitatively, structured input resulted in negligible changes to accuracy and F1 (within ±0.01 of unstructured input), and error patterns remained similar. Analysis of model attention weights and error cases showed that the model already focused on key fields in the original invoice text, and the additional structuring did not provide new or more salient information. For example, invoices with both structured and unstructured formats yielded nearly identical prediction confidence and error patterns, suggesting that the inherent regularity of invoice formats already supports effective model attention. However, our structuring approaches may not capture more complex or inconsistent invoice layouts found in some industries (e.g., invoices with nested tables or highly variable field locations). More advanced structuring techniques, such as automated field extraction (see e.g., Palm et al., 2022) or layout-aware models (Xu et al., 2020), could be explored in future work to address these cases.

In summary, our findings indicate that in-house SLMs like SBERT can deliver high accuracy and generalisability for invoice categorisation, with the added benefits of cost control and data confidentiality. The geometric analysis of embeddings provides insight into model decision-making and highlights the importance of vendor-driven clusters. However, our approach may be less effective in domains where vendor information is less predictive. Potential biases in the dataset, such as overrepresentation of certain industries or vendors, may limit generalisability to less common scenarios. In real-world deployment, these biases could result in lower accuracy for underrepresented sectors or new vendors. Mitigation strategies include targeted data augmentation, periodic retraining with new data, and incorporating domain adaptation techniques to improve robustness. Anticipated integration challenges in production workflows include aligning model outputs with existing accounting systems, handling edge cases such as invoices from new vendors or with ambiguous descriptions, and ensuring ongoing data quality. Addressing these may require fallback rules, human-in-the-loop review, or periodic retraining
